title: Otto Vass case brings out the top legal eagles
article: They are, what, the four horsemen of the apocalypse?
No, no, no. That would be war, famine, pestilence and death. As an analogy, a bit harsh, even for a quartet of swooping cop lawyers.

Call them The Four Silver Tops then, a superannuated boy-band of legal eagles Gary Clewley, Harry Black, Earl Levy and Mark Sandler. Now playing in courtroom 6-1 of the University Ave. courthouse, one more debonairly suave than the next.

Representing, respectively Constables Robert LeMaitre, Nam Le, Phillip Duncan and Filippo Bevilacqua, all of whom have pleaded not guilty to one count each of manslaughter in the death of _Otto_ _Vass_, an indisputably disturbed 55-year-old who died Aug. 9, 2000, in circumstances that have barely begun to emerge from testimony.

Rare are the occasions when this kind of top-drawer robed assembly will be pulled together in a courtroom anywhere in Canada. They are, formally, all on the same side, lined up against crown attorneys Desmond McGarry and Roger Pinnock, although their clients, from the evidence presented thus far, have varying degrees of involvement in the disputed events of that early-morning episode at a west-end 7-Eleven.

The crown contends a physical altercation outside the convenience store, shortly after midnight, with "multiple blows" received by _Vass_, resulted in injuries - specifically, escaping fat particles clogging the bloodstream and causing an embolism in the lungs - that killed _Vass_.

Levy, for one, has characterized the confrontation as more a battle than a beating, with an enraged _Vass_ exhibiting near super- human strength as he resisted attempts by the officers to subdue him, following a telephoned complaint to police. Clearly, this is the defensive gist of all the lawyers involved, as they seek to convince a jury that the constables used only reasonable force commensurate to the situation, and that such use of force did not contribute to _Vass_' death.

It's early days in the trial yet - expected to last up to two months - and the Silver Tops appear to be barely warming up to the gig in their exchanges with witnesses. None of those summoned thus far actually witnessed the critical events that occurred outside the 7-Eleven and no security cameras captured the scene. What was captured on video, replayed endlessly for the jury, are images from inside the store, when _Vass_ was still very much alive and not much of a threat to anyone, albeit decidedly odd in his behaviour and fresh off another peculiar, also violent, episode.

Court has now heard from the three young men - just mooks cruising around the neighbourhood in their SUV - who had the misfortune of assuming peripheral roles in unfolding events. They were parked outside the 7-Eleven when, each has testified, a guy came out of nowhere and slugged one of them, Mike Massa, in the head, yelling "Are you the f---ers?"

That incident had been unprovoked, although _Vass_ was palpably upset about something, which may have been real or imagined. This is a man with documented mental health problems, violent exchanges in the past, told doctors he had a microchip in his brain that was controlled by microwaves and who had, earlier that evening, jumped out of his van, causing it to hit a wall, complaining there was a bomb inside the vehicle and that he could smell napalm.

The three men, understandably peeved, followed _Vass_ into the store, boxing him in near a coffee counter, where one of them, Nelson Cerqueira, delivered a "glancing" blow to the upper body. _Vass_, court has heard, was wielding a pricing gun at one point, a length of counter plastic at another point.

Having made their point, and ostensibly not wanting further trouble, the three men left (one of them returning briefly to collect his baseball cap), hung out for a couple of hours longer at one of their homes, then retired for the night. It was not until the next morning, listening to the news, that they discovered their weirdo assailant had died. Not that any of them went to police to report their part in the final hour of _Vass_' life - details that were elicited only when Special Investigations Unit officers came knocking on their doors nearly a week later.

There has been no evidence yet to explain _Vass_' behaviour, if a rational explanation even exists. After punching Massa, _Vass_ withdrew into the 7-Eleven. Employee Asiya Semet picks up the story from the witness stand yesterday "He ran into the store, he seemed in a hurry. I noticed some blood and scratches on his forehead and on his nose. He said, 'Some guys are chasing me. ... Can I have a cup of coffee?'"
When the young men followed, _Vass_, Semet told court, shouted at them "You out! You out! I don't want to go out!"

Semet and the other two women working that shift wanted the whole bunch out of the store. But _Vass_ wouldn't leave, which is when one of them phoned police. "Now you can go out of the store," Semet said she told _Vass_ after the three young men had exited. He responded "No, I don't want to. I want to calm down. I want to drink another cup of coffee."

_Vass_ told Semet he didn't know why the men had attacked him. Within 10 minutes, two officers - LeMaitre and Duncan - had arrived on the scene. Semet told court the conversation between _Vass_ and the cops was brief and without rancour. "_Otto_ _Vass_ just followed them out, very willingly, no resistance."

Semet, noticing a bulb in the coffee maker had been broken, trailed after the group, demanding that somebody make good for the damage, however small. The officers assured her _Vass_ would pay. And that was it.

Semet didn't even notice the arrival of other officers, responding to a dispatcher call for help at the scene. This is when, allegedly, the struggle ensued. That struggle took, according to a time-line presented in court, all of 44 seconds, followed by an "all in order call" to the dispatcher.
But three minutes later, another call was made, this time requesting an ambulance because _Vass_ had stopped breathing.

Semet had also provided the court with a description of _Vass_ as she remembered him, in light-coloured T-shirt and shorts. But when she was asked to view the surveillance video, she seemed puzzled by the appearance of a man in a dark T-shirt and shorts. "I didn't even notice he was there."
That was _Vass_, Semet was informed.
"That's Mr. _Vass_? My impression was very different."
